name: Daria Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and have spent years on the electricity company’s power line crews, though I am still one of the ordinary repair hands rather than a team lead. My vocational certificate and apprenticeship left me with a habit of marking the pole number in pencil on the work sheet before we unload the truck. I like a clean repair that stays fixed, and I am tired of night callouts after bad weather. My partner and I have grown children; we have talked about finishing full-time work around sixty-eight if the income is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that the faster forms are fine as long as we still check the line at the pole. A neat AI work order will not tell my hands whether a power line insulator is cracked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never use AI tools and do not see much reason to start for a small form change. My lineworker pay is high, we have over six months saved, and there are plenty of similar jobs nearby, so the retirement question can wait for real numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the same repair shifts and mark the pole number on each work sheet as I do now. This year I would request a retirement income estimate and compare it with our household costs before fixing any date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this one. I have a steady wage and a little room to decide how long I keep climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mark the pole number by hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rushed dispatch sheet once sent us to the next pole along the road. My pencil mark makes me stop and check the tag on site before unloading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change your planned finish around sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a real retirement estimate and a discussion with my partner. We have saved well, but more than six months of expenses is not the same as a lifetime of income.

say: A **faster** form is acceptable if crews still check the actual line.
I would **keep** my pencil pole-number check before each repair.
think: **High** pay, strong savings and many nearby jobs make a small AI change manageable.
I do **not** use AI and will not set a retirement date without income figures.
do: **Keep** repair shifts and mark pole numbers on work sheets.
**Request** retirement income estimate and compare it with household costs.
feel: **Calm** about work, with room to decide later retirement timing.
S0.quote: A neat AI work order will not tell my hands whether a power line insulator is cracked.
fieldNote: She **relies** on a physical pole-tag habit and does not use AI tools.
A **strong** cushion supports calm, but she distinguishes temporary savings from lifetime retirement income.

steps.text: Keep repair shifts and mark pole numbers on work sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say booking software can send a crew, but it should name a person who answers when the wrong pole is listed. I would want the depot to test the new schedule against actual travel and isolation times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is hands-on repair, so desk workers face the first disruption. Still, if the company uses software times to cut callout hours, I might lose part of the high wage that makes our planned finish possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a month of work orders with actual arrival and isolation times and give the comparison to our supervisor. During the first year I would request written callout rules and compare any lost paid hours against our retirement budget before looking for another firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible hours cut, even with our savings. I am not interested in arguing with a screen while a line waits for a safe isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What entry would show an unfair time target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week our crew had to place barriers before a repair across a narrow road. A power line schedule that skips road barriers has already spent time my crew still has to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the scheduling system to correct an error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hand the marked work order to the dispatcher and have the crew lead confirm the fix. I do not use AI tools, and I would keep my field record until the correction appears on the next sheet.

say: A **named** dispatcher should answer when booking software sends crews to wrong poles.
I would **compare** software times with real travel and isolation work.
think: **Desk** jobs change first, but reduced callout hours could cut my higher wage.
**Savings** give time, yet an hour loss could alter our retirement budget.
do: **Record** actual arrival and isolation times for one month.
**Request** written callout rules and compare lost hours with retirement budget.
**Keep** field work orders until wrong dispatch entries are corrected.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour loss, despite financial room to respond.
S1.quote: A power line schedule that skips road barriers has already spent time my crew still has to work.
fieldNote: She **tests** outputs against field records without adopting the AI scheduling tool herself.
Her **worry** is possible paid-hour loss, not a claim that field repairs disappear now.

steps.text: Keep one month of arrival and isolation records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that thinking AI by 2028 can change dispatch, but capable hands-on robots around 2031 need real field proof before touching a power line. The crew must still be able to stop an unsafe repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be sixty when the thinking system arrives and sixty-three when robots can climb. Our savings of more than six months will not buy five years of power line wages if a robot takes the callouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the safety manager this year for a written crew stop rule and keep a record of robot field faults if trials begin. In the first year after 2028, if paid callouts fall, I would compare written offers from nearby electricity companies while keeping my repair shifts; I would also recalculate whether our sixty-eight plan still covers costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible income gap, not certain that my job ends. We have nearby options, but I do not want to gamble five working years on a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a robot field fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine choosing the wrong pole tag or gripping a damaged crossarm would count. I would note the site and stop the repair before someone calls the trial complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a nearby offer need to include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would need enough pay and a written safety role that still uses my repair skills. I would not leave for a notice that says only that applications are open.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches dispatch by 2028; capable line robots follow around 2031.
I would **require** field proof and crew stop authority before robot repairs.
think: **Robot** callouts could remove up to five planned years of higher earnings.
**Strong** savings and nearby firms help, but do not replace those wages.
do: **Request** written crew stop rule from safety manager this year.
**Compare** nearby written lineworker offers if paid callouts fall after 2028.
**Recalculate** retirement budget if callout income falls.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost earnings, with local alternatives still available.
S2.quote: Our savings of more than six months will not buy five years of power line wages if a robot takes the callouts.
fieldNote: She **sees** a possible long wage gap at sixty-three without assuming certain job loss.
Her **job** search depends on actual lost callouts and written comparable offers.

steps.text: Compare nearby written lineworker offers if callout pay falls
Keep repair shifts while evaluating actual offers and income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2031 changes dispatch when I am sixty-three, with capable robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. A field inspector should touch the damaged power line hardware before signing a robot repair complete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sixty-six is nearer my hoped-for finish at sixty-eight, but two years of wages still matter. I could inspect completed line repairs if it is a real paid field job, though I have no wish to learn AI software just to approve a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company this year for the field inspection duties, rate and whether a supervised course is paid. If it posts a local inspection job at least matching my current wage and funds hands-on training, I would take the course before 2031 and apply when the role opens; otherwise I would keep repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possibly losing two years of pay, because I would need to see the terms. I can learn a physical checking duty after a good trial without becoming the person who trusts a screen blindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should a hands-on inspection lesson include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a damaged crossarm and an isolation marker that is easy to miss. The learner should check the pole and work sheet before approving a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection rate is lower than your line rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay with the crew and keep the ordinary wage while I review our retirement numbers. A title is not worth two years of lost pay.

say: The **longer** lead gives time for paid human inspection before robots reach lines around 2034.
I would **judge** a real field role by its wage and duties.
think: **Two** years of earnings between sixty-six and my hoped-for finish still matter.
I can **learn** hands-on inspection but will not adopt AI software on a promise.
do: **Request** inspection duties, wage and paid-course terms this year.
**Take** supervised field course before 2031 if local matching-pay job is posted and training funded.
**Apply** when actual local inspection job opens at current wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost wages, with time to examine a physical role.
S3.quote: A field inspector should touch the damaged power line hardware before signing a robot repair complete.
fieldNote: Her **openness** extends to physical inspection after proof, not to untested AI controls.
The **course** and application require funding, a posted local job and matching pay.

steps.text: Take supervised field course before 2031 if funded and matching-pay local job posted
Apply for posted local inspector role if wage matches current line pay
Keep repair shifts if inspection terms are inadequate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI in 2036 and capable line robots around 2039 come after my hoped-for finish at sixty-eight, if our retirement figures work. The company should still teach younger workers to check a physical pole before a machine plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives I may already be leaving full-time work, and at seventy-one for robots I hope to be away from storm climbs. I cannot promise either without a real retirement income estimate, but the long timeline gives me breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my line shifts now and request a fresh retirement estimate each year. If it covers household costs at sixty-eight, I would finish full-time on our existing plan; if it does not, I would look for paid ground inspection work at my company before ending the repair rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the machine date, cautious about the retirement figure. I can keep the trade I know while the sums become clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach apprentices after leaving the repair rota?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might teach on paid ground shifts if I still need wages. My pencil mark on a power line work sheet may outlast the AI plan if the pole tag is wrong. I would not promise regular unpaid lessons while we still need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make ground inspection worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need written duties, workable hours and pay enough to close the gap in our household budget. I would compare that offer with a few nearby lineworker roles before accepting.

say: The **decade** places capable robots after my conditional full-time finish at sixty-eight.
**Younger** crews still need physical pole checks.
think: A **retirement** income estimate must cover living costs before I leave repair shifts.
**Paid** ground inspection is a fallback if household income remains short.
do: **Keep** line shifts and update retirement income estimate annually.
**Finish** full-time at planned sixty-eight only if income covers costs.
**Seek** paid ground inspection if income is short and actual duties and pay work.
feel: **Calm** about later robots, cautious about retirement income.
S4.quote: My pencil mark on a power line work sheet may outlast the AI plan if the pole tag is wrong.
fieldNote: Her **longer** timeline permits a conditional exit on the existing plan.
**Ground** work is a paid fallback requiring a real offer with suitable duties and wages, rather than an assumed guaranteed position.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and update retirement estimate each year
Leave full-time line work at planned sixty-eight if income covers costs
Seek paid ground inspection if retirement income is short and offer suits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because line robots could reach repairs when I am sixty-three, five years before I hope to finish full-time work. A written stop rule, real fault records and comparable nearby job offers would help. I will not give a robot five years of my power line pay just because a trial film looks smooth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the company will do when a robot chooses the wrong pole. The repair crew needs the authority to stop it, and the next crew needs the fault record. A good wage is worth protecting, but nobody should have to earn it by taking an unsafe shortcut.

headlineQuote: I will not give a robot five years of my power line pay just because a trial film looks smooth.
portrait: **Daria** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company lineworker with a vocational certificate, apprenticeship and a pencil-marked pole check.
**Higher** pay, more than six months of savings and many nearby jobs support her partner and grown children as retirement nears.
She does **not** use AI tools, but she will consider proven physical inspection work with paid training and matching wages.
She **hopes** to finish full-time around sixty-eight if income permits; the 2031 robot date puts five working years at stake.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031, five years before her conditional full-time finish.
whatWouldHelp: A **written** crew stop rule, real fault records and comparable nearby job offers would help her respond.
